questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Let L={0^n1^n:0≤n≤20}. Is L regular?

options.label: No; matching two counts is always nonregular.

questions.explanation: The bound 20 is fixed, so only 21 words occur. Unbounded equality is the obstruction in {0^n1^n:n≥0}.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Which recognizer pairing matches the language-class table?
questions.explanation: DFAs characterize regular languages. The table associates context-free languages with pushdown automata, context-sensitive languages with linearly bounded nondeterministic Turing machines, and recursively enumerable languages with Turing machines; larger models can also recognize regular languages.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Why does a regular token vocabulary not imply a regular programming-language grammar?

options.label: A finite alphabet makes all syntax regular.
Every token stream must already be a legal program.
Combining tokens into nested structures may require unbounded matching.

questions.explanation: Lexical patterns and full program structure are different languages. Unbounded matching of nested delimiters cannot in general be handled by a DFA alone.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: If L is not regular, which conclusion follows?

options.label: No finite DFA recognizes exactly L.

questions.explanation: Nonregular means outside the expressive power of finite automata and formal regexes. It does not imply uncomputability or infinite individual words.

questions.title: Regular language
questions.question: Can a regular language have a nonregular subset?

options.label: No; regularity passes to all subsets.
Only if the regular language is finite.
Only if the subset contains infinite words.

questions.explanation: Σ* is regular and contains every language over Σ, including nonregular ones. A finite language cannot have a nonregular subset because its subsets are finite.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: Which is enough to prove L regular?

options.label: Fail to find a pumping-lemma contradiction.
Show L is a subset of Σ*.
Construct a regex and prove its language equals L.

questions.explanation: Every language over Σ is a subset of Σ*. Exact equality with a regex language is a regularity proof; finite tests and unsuccessful proof attempts are not.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: What must be established when claiming L=L(R)?

options.label: Only one word of L matches R.
Only L and L(R) are both infinite.
Only every word of L matches R.
Every word of L matches R and every match of R belongs to L.

questions.explanation: Two set inclusions establish equality. A construction that accepts too much or too little does not recognize the target exactly.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: Which regex proves that unary words whose length is divisible by 4 are regular?
questions.explanation: (aaaa)* builds lengths 0,4,8,... . aaaa* means at least three a symbols, a*aaaa means at least four, and aaaa has one length only.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: Which expression describes unary words whose length is not divisible by 3?
questions.explanation: The residue is 1 or 2 modulo 3. ε is excluded because zero is divisible by 3.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: A proof uses {0},{1}, union, concatenation and star. What justifies the last construction step?

options.label: A chosen word has finite length
The language has a finite alphabet
A graph could probably be drawn
Closure of regular languages under the operation actually used

questions.explanation: Base languages are regular, and each subsequent operation must preserve regularity. A finite alphabet alone does not suffice.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: Which is the correct regex for nonempty binary words with equal first and last symbols, including length one?
questions.explanation: The two one-symbol words need separate alternatives. The endpoint alternatives require at least two symbols, and ε has no first or last symbol.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: Which regex describes an even number of 1s with arbitrary 0s, including zero 1s?
questions.explanation: A leading 0* covers all-zero words, and each repeated block contributes two 1s. The second expression misses nonempty all-zero words.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: To prove Σ*{0^n1^n:n≥1}Σ*=Σ*01Σ*, which missing direction matters?

options.label: The nonregular middle language forces the product to be nonregular.
Every word containing 01 is included by choosing n=1.
Every word is in both languages.

questions.explanation: The forward direction uses the boundary 01 inside each 0^n1^n. The reverse direction uses n=1; nonregular components can yield a regular product.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: For positive integers m,n, which construction describes lengths divisible by both m and n?
questions.explanation: A common multiple is a multiple of lcm(m,n). Union expresses 'or'; a single concatenation has fixed length m+n.

questions.title: Regular-language proofs
questions.question: A proposed DFA passes 100 test words. What is the strongest justified conclusion?

options.label: It recognizes the intended language for all inputs.
It cannot contain a dead state.
It has passed those tests; a general correctness argument is still needed.

questions.explanation: Finite tests may miss a longer counterexample. State invariants or exact equivalence checking can establish correctness for all inputs.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: If R and S are regular over the same alphabet, which is guaranteed regular?

options.label: Every arbitrary infinite union of regular languages

questions.explanation: Difference is a closure operation. Arbitrary subsets, supersets and infinite unions may be nonregular.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: Which identity correctly expresses intersection using union and complement?
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law requires complementing each input and the union. All complements use the same universe Σ*.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: Which identity expresses set difference?
questions.explanation: Keep words in R that are not in S. Difference is not generally symmetric.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: If R is regular, what can be said about its reversal R^rev?

options.label: It is always equal to R.
It is regular only if ε∈R.

questions.explanation: Regular languages are closed under reversal. For R={ab}, its reversal is {ba}, so equality is not guaranteed.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: Let N be nonregular. Which expression is necessarily nonregular?
questions.explanation: If the complement were regular, complementing again would make N regular. The other three expressions are Σ*, ∅ and ∅.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: If N is nonregular and F is finite, what is N∪F?
questions.explanation: If N∪F were regular, then N=((N∪F)\F)∪(N∩F) would be regular because N∩F is finite. This is a contradiction.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: If N is nonregular and R is regular, what can be said about N∩R?

options.label: It may be regular or nonregular.

questions.explanation: Taking R=∅ gives ∅; taking R=Σ* gives N. Closure does not apply when one input is already nonregular.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: Which example disproves 'a regular union must have regular components'?
questions.explanation: A counterexample must satisfy the premise and violate the conclusion. Only the first has a regular result with a nonregular component.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: Which claim is valid about arbitrary infinite unions?

options.label: They are always regular by union closure.
They are finite whenever the alphabet is finite.
They can be nonregular even when every component is regular.

questions.explanation: The union over n≥0 of the singletons {0^n1^n} is nonregular, although each singleton is regular. Closure guarantees finite unions.

questions.title: Closure properties
questions.question: If R^rev is regular, what follows about R?

options.label: R may be nonregular because all converse closure statements fail.
R is regular because reversal twice returns R.

questions.explanation: Reversal, like complement, is an involution. Some backward arguments are valid; do not generalize failures of union or star to every operation.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Which is a standard nonregular language from this module?
questions.explanation: The first requires equal unbounded block lengths. The others have regexes or are finite.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Why is 'L is infinite, so L is nonregular' invalid?
questions.explanation: Infinite cardinality is compatible with a finite repeating automaton. Individual words remain finite.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: In a closure-based contradiction, which language should be used as a filter?

options.label: A finite sample of accepted words
The target itself without further justification
A known regular language that isolates a known nonregular part

questions.explanation: Assuming the target regular then intersecting with a known regular filter forces a regular result, contradicting a known nonregular identity.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Let L={w∈{a,b,c,d}*:|w|a+|w|b<|w|c+|w|d}. What is L∩a*c*?
questions.explanation: The filter removes b and d and puts all a symbols before c symbols, leaving the strict comparison i<j.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Let P={a^p:p prime}. Why is a*\P nonregular?

options.label: If it were regular, complementing within a* would make P regular.
Removing any infinite subset destroys regularity.

questions.explanation: The argument uses complement closure and known nonregularity of P. The other reasons are not valid general rules.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Let L={a^i b^j:i,j≥0 and i or j is prime}. What is L∩a*?
questions.explanation: The filter forces j=0, which is not prime. Thus membership depends exactly on i being prime.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Let P be the unary prime-length language and E=(aa)*. What is (E∪P)∩((aa)*a|aa)?
questions.explanation: The filter retains odd lengths and length 2. These remove nonprime even lengths while preserving every prime length, so the intersection is P.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Which statement is correct about 'DFAs cannot count'?

options.label: They cannot distinguish ε from a.
They cannot recognize exactly three a symbols.
They can track fixed remainders and bounded counts, but not arbitrary exact counts.

questions.explanation: A finite set of states can store a finite number of possibilities, such as parity or counts up to three plus overflow.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: Which language is regular despite mentioning equal-sized blocks?
questions.explanation: The first is exactly the language containing 01, since n=1 is allowed and every larger block contains 01. The surrounding freedom changes the problem.

questions.title: Nonregular languages
questions.question: If no regex has occurred to you for L, what may you conclude?

options.label: L requires infinitely many alphabet symbols.
Nothing about regularity without further reasoning.

questions.explanation: Failure to discover a representation is not a proof that none exists. Use a construction or a valid nonregularity argument.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: Which components specify a DFA in the lecture's order?
questions.explanation: The five components are alphabet, states, transition function, start state and final-state set. Other tuple orders are acceptable only when explicitly defined.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: What makes a finite automaton deterministic?

options.label: Each state-symbol pair has exactly one next state.
It has exactly one accepting state.

questions.explanation: Determinism concerns the transition choice. A DFA may have several final states, loops, and rejected words.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: Can a DFA have no final states?

options.label: No; it must have exactly one.

questions.explanation: With F=∅, no run ends in an accepting state, including the empty-input run.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: A one-state complete DFA has its single state accepting. What language does it recognize?
questions.explanation: All transitions loop to its only state, and that state is accepting before and after every finite input.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: For 'an odd number of b symbols' over {a,b}, what information is sufficient?
questions.explanation: Two states track even versus odd b counts. a preserves parity; b toggles it.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: For binary numeric value modulo 3, what update follows reading bit d from remainder r?
questions.explanation: Appending a bit multiplies the previous value by 2 and adds the bit. Length modulo 3 and number of 1s modulo 3 are different tasks.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: To recognize words ending in zz over {x,y,z}, which state information is sufficient?

options.label: Total number of z symbols ever read
Whether the current suffix matches zero, one, or at least two trailing z symbols

questions.explanation: A new x or y resets the suffix; z extends it. Arbitrarily many total z symbols do not imply the word ends in zz.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: Does a DFA need a separate state for every possible input word?

options.label: No; prefixes with the same relevant future behavior can share a state.
Yes; otherwise different words cannot be processed.

questions.explanation: Finite-state compression is the point of the model. Many different prefixes lead to the same state.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: Which change preserves the language of a DFA?

options.label: Consistently rename every state in transitions, start state and final set.

questions.explanation: State names are labels, not semantics. The other changes can alter which words are accepted; flipping finals complements a complete DFA.

questions.title: DFA
questions.question: What must be checked when a drawn DFA has omitted transitions?

options.label: Whether missing transitions are ε moves.
Whether a rejecting sink was intended; formally the DFA must be completed.
Whether it has too many final states.

questions.explanation: The course definition uses a total δ. Missing labeled transitions may be diagram shorthand for a rejecting sink, but are not ε transitions.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: When does a DFA accept w?

options.label: After all of w is read, the current state is final.
Whenever the start state has an outgoing edge.
As soon as any final state is visited.

questions.explanation: Acceptance is tested at the end of the entire input. A later transition can leave a final state.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: What does M recognizes L mean?

options.label: M has a final state named L.
M accepts exactly the words in L.
M accepts all words in L, possibly others.
M accepts at least one word in L.

questions.explanation: Recognition requires both accepting every member and rejecting every nonmember.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: For a DFA, when is ε accepted?

options.label: Exactly when there is a self-loop

questions.explanation: No symbols are consumed, so the run remains at the start state. Other final states need not be reachable without input.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: A DFA recognizes binary words ending in 1. It reads 10. What happens?

options.label: Reject; every two-symbol word is rejected.
Accept; a final state was reached after the first symbol.

questions.explanation: The prefix 1 is accepted, but the full word 10 is not. Acceptance is not permanent unless the automaton's structure makes it so.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: A DFA recognizes binary words with no adjacent 1s. Which word is rejected?
questions.explanation: 0110 contains 11. Isolated 1s are permitted, and ε has no forbidden adjacent pair.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: A DFA accepts every word in L but also accepts a word outside L. Which statement is true?

options.label: It recognizes L because it has no false negatives.
It recognizes L if the extra word is short.
It recognizes L if L is infinite.

questions.explanation: Exact recognition rules out both false positives and false negatives, regardless of word length or language size.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: For the DFA q0:0→q0,1→q1; q1:0→q0,1→q1, with start q0 and F={q1}, where does 1011 end?
questions.explanation: The state sequence is q0,q1,q0,q1,q1. Only q1 is final.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: If a complete DFA rejects w, what does flipping all final-state memberships do?

options.label: It may have no run on w.
It still rejects w because transitions are unchanged.
It accepts only if w is nonempty.

questions.explanation: The unique complete run is unchanged, but the status of its ending state is reversed, even for ε.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: Can two different DFAs recognize the same language?

options.label: Only if their transition tables are identical.
Yes, even with different numbers of states.
No; the language fixes every state name.

questions.explanation: Unreachable or equivalent states can create larger presentations of the same language. A minimal complete DFA is unique only up to consistent renaming.

questions.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
questions.question: Which claim is stronger than 'M accepts 101'?

options.label: M accepts at least one word.

questions.explanation: Recognizing {101} additionally requires rejection of every other word. Acceptance of 101 alone only establishes one membership fact.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: How many start states does a standard DFA have?
questions.explanation: The definition specifies one distinguished q0∈Q. Multiple final states are allowed.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: How many final states may a DFA have?

options.label: At least one but never all

questions.explanation: F is any subset of Q, including ∅ and Q.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: Can the start state also be final?

options.label: Yes, and then ε is accepted.
Yes, but then no nonempty input is accepted.
Yes, but only in an NFA.
No; start and final are disjoint roles.

questions.explanation: These roles can overlap. Acceptance of nonempty words still depends on transitions.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: In a DFA for no adjacent 1s, what can a nonfinal sink record?

options.label: The last symbol is 0 and no violation occurred.

questions.explanation: Once 11 occurs, no suffix can remove it. That irreversible violation makes a rejecting sink appropriate.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: Which statement about final states is true?

options.label: They are always reached only at end of input.
They must loop on every symbol.
They may have outgoing transitions to nonfinal states.

questions.explanation: A complete DFA defines outgoing transitions from all states. A final state merely indicates acceptance if the input ends there.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: In a parity DFA over {a,b}, qEven records an even number of a symbols. What should b do?
questions.explanation: b does not change the a count. The automaton still consumes b.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: What does an unreachable state contribute to the recognized language?

options.label: Nothing, because no run from q0 visits it.

questions.explanation: Reachability is measured from the designated start state. Removing unreachable states preserves all actual runs.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: Can a sink state be accepting?

options.label: Only when the alphabet is empty.
Yes; then every continuation from it is accepted.

questions.explanation: A sink is defined by self-loops on every symbol, not by final status. A rejecting sink is a particular kind of sink.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: Why can states 'first symbol 0, last symbol 0' and 'first symbol 1, last symbol 1' still be different?

options.label: They are both final, so they cannot be compared.
Their printed names must have equal length to merge.
A common suffix can make one accepted and the other rejected.
Every final state requires its own alphabet.

questions.explanation: Both prefixes currently meet the endpoint condition, but appending 0 preserves equality only for the first-symbol-0 state. Current acceptance alone does not determine equivalence.

questions.title: State, start state and final state
questions.question: If every reachable state is final in a complete DFA, what is recognized?
questions.explanation: Every complete finite run ends in a reachable state, all of which are accepting. Unreachable nonfinal states do not change this.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: How many input symbols does one standard DFA transition consume?
questions.explanation: A standard DFA transition is indexed by one symbol. ε transitions belong to the NFA model used here.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: What does an edge labeled 0,1 usually abbreviate over Σ={0,1}?

options.label: Two transitions with the same source and destination
A choice between accepting and rejecting

questions.explanation: The comma lists alternative single-symbol labels, not a two-symbol word.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: Over Σ={0,1}, is a single edge labeled 01 a standard DFA transition?

options.label: No; it represents two input symbols.
Only if the destination is final.
Yes; all finite words are DFA labels.

questions.explanation: Standard DFA edges consume one symbol. A path with two edges, or a GNFA edge with regex 01, can express this behavior.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: If a DFA reads a word of length n, how many symbol transitions occur?
questions.explanation: There are n consumed symbols and n transitions. Including the initial state gives n+1 state visits.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: If a loop labeled a is traversed three times, what input is consumed?
questions.explanation: A self-loop still consumes its label each time. Returning to the same state does not mean consuming nothing.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: Does a transition on a inspect the next unread symbol after a too?

options.label: Yes; it automatically reads two symbols.
Only when a appears twice in the alphabet.
No; its destination depends only on current state and a.
Only when the destination is final.

questions.explanation: The standard DFA transition function has two inputs: current state and current symbol. Any needed history is encoded in the state.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: For Σ={ID,PLUS,NUM} with each listed token kind atomic, may an edge labeled PLUS consume one symbol?

options.label: Only if the source is final.
Yes; atomicity comes from the alphabet definition.
No; PLUS has four printed letters.

questions.explanation: Symbol names can be multi-character strings on paper. They represent one alphabet element when declared atomic.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: Which edge consumes no input?

options.label: An ε edge in an NFA
An edge into a final state labeled a

questions.explanation: Consumption depends on the label, not on whether the state changes or is accepting.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: If δ(q,a)=q, which statement is true?

options.label: a is consumed and the state remains q.

questions.explanation: A self-loop updates the input position while preserving the state; no acceptance status is implied.

questions.title: Symbols and input consumption
questions.question: When computing a transition, which distinction matters?

options.label: Equal printed names always mean equal mathematical objects.
A state name is not an input symbol merely because both are written 'a'.
Every alphabet symbol belongs to F.

questions.explanation: Q and Σ play different roles. Clear naming prevents confusing state identities with the symbols used to select transitions.
